description: We are a team passionate about technology, the environment and social impact. Every year, wildfires destroy thousands of hectares across Peru’s Amazon, its Andes and its cloud forests (the selva alta). They harm biodiversity, air quality and the communities that depend on these ecosystems. We believe NASA satellite data can help us detect, prevent and respond to these fires faster and more intelligently.
summary: Every year Peru has a burning season, but is this one normal, or is it changing? NinaWillay answers that question. NASA's MODIS sensors have recorded fire hot spots since 2000, but since 2012 the newer VIIRS satellites see much smaller fires and detect 5 to 9 times more hot spots. Put side by side, the raw records make it look as if fires exploded in 2012, so the old and new data can't be compared. We built a translator between them. While both satellites flew together, we learned their "exchange rate", season by season. We tested it on five years the model never saw, with an error of about 4%, and used it to convert the 2002–2011 MODIS record to the VIIRS scale. The result is one consistent fire history for Peru from 2002 to 2026. Our web app turns it into a map and a monthly calendar that compares every month with its normal. That way fire brigades, local authorities and rural communities can spot an unusual season early and prepare in time.
details:
Our goals

1. Harmonize MODIS and VIIRS into one consistent hot spot series for Peru, with honest error margins.

2. Build a responsive web app where anyone can pick a region and a period and see the hot spots and how they compare with normal.

3. Make it multilingual and accessible, for firefighters, local authorities and people in rural areas of Peru.

What does it do?

- One fire history for Peru, 2002–2026, by week, month and year, and on a map grid. Every value says whether it is estimated (2002–2011, translated from MODIS) or observed (VIIRS, from 2012), and comes with an error margin. Data from August–November 2026 is labeled preliminary (near-real-time data that NASA will later replace).

- A fire map of hot spots per 100 km², by year and month.

- A fire calendar (year × month) that compares each month with the same month in 2003–2024, from "much less fire" to "record fire". The colors are colorblind-friendly.

- Open data: every view can be downloaded as CSV.

How does it work?

1. Collect. We download NASA FIRMS hot spots for Peru from four NASA satellites: Aqua and Terra (MODIS), and Suomi NPP and NOAA-20 (VIIRS).

2. Clean. We keep only vegetation fires with good confidence, and remove places that are always "hot" but aren't fires (volcanoes, industry, gas flares).

3. Compare. We count hot spots per week. From 2012 to 2022, Aqua and VIIRS flew together and passed over Peru at the same time of day, so we measured how many hot spots VIIRS sees for each one Aqua sees. The answer depends on the season: about 5× at the August–September peak and about 9× in the rainy season, when fires are small and harder to see.

4. Test. We learned the exchange rate only from 2012–2017 and tested it on 2018–2022, years the model never saw. The total was off by 3.8%, and it followed the week-to-week ups and downs closely (correlation 0.98). The NOAA-20 satellite independently agrees with Suomi NPP within about ±5% per year.

5. Translate and publish. We apply the exchange rate to the 2002–2011 MODIS record, join it with real VIIRS data from 2012, and turn the result into the map and calendar of the web app.

What benefits does it have?

- Knowing what "normal" looks like. Without a long comparable record, nobody can say whether a fire season is unusual. Now Peru has one record covering more than 20 years.

- Hidden findings. In the raw data, 2005 looks like a quiet year. Harmonized, 2005 was Peru's worst fire year since 2002 (≈ 101,000 hot spots on today's VIIRS scale; even the low end of its range is above 2024, ≈ 93,000).

- Early warning. With preliminary data, October 2026 shows clearly above-normal fire activity in Cusco after a calm August. That is exactly the kind of signal the calendar is designed to catch.

- Urgency. The bridge between the two records has to be built now: Aqua's orbit is drifting, and Suomi NPP stopped delivering data on 2 November 2026. NOAA-20 keeps the record going.

What do we hope to achieve?

Give fire brigades, regional governments, protected-area managers and rural communities in Peru, a reliable baseline to spot abnormal burning early, prepare before the August–September peak, and check over the years whether prevention works. Next steps:

- Region-specific exchange rates (Coast, Andes, Amazon);

- Validation against NASA's MODIS Burned Area product (MCD64A1);

- Automatic near-real-time updates with NOAA-20 and NOAA-21;

- The same method for any country with a FIRMS archive.

What makes it creative?

We treat the two satellites like two currencies and measure an exchange rate that changes with the season: in the rainy season, the old satellite sees only about 1 in 9 of the hot spots the new one sees; at the peak, about 1 in 5. And instead of a chart only experts can read, the result is a calendar any brigade can understand at a glance.

Tools

- Data processing: Python 3 (pandas, NumPy, statsmodels, Matplotlib, PyYAML, PyArrow).

- Web app (frontend): React 19, TypeScript, TanStack Start/Router, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Lucide icons.

- Maps: Leaflet, MapLibre GL, OpenFreeMap base maps, AWS Terrain Tiles (relief), Turf.js (geospatial analysis).

- Data in the app: static JSON files (pipeline schema 1.2), PapaParse (CSV download).

- Languages: Spanish, English and Quechua; Quechua refined with the SimiAru open lexicon.

- Testing and code quality: Vitest, ESLint, Prettier.

- Deployment: Vercel (built with Nitro), GitHub.

- Team work: GitHub, GitHub Desktop, Google Colab, Figma.

AI assistance

Claude (Anthropic) via Claude Code for the data pipeline (Python code for cleaning, static-source mask, aggregation and GLM calibration; data-gap and sensor cross-checks; frontend data contract), frontend code, translations and documentation; Lovable for the initial project scaffold.
